options_ranked.title: Contract-Safe Synthetic Blend Price Recovery and Incentive Reset
options_ranked.description: Introduce indexation or selective price increases on eligible non-anchor Synthetic Blend business, and schedule anchor-account changes only after their contractual locks expire. Rebalance discretionary incentives toward Synthetic Blend SKUs with demonstrated superior realized contribution. Synthetic Blend currently has a higher margin than Conventional Engine Oil and Value, but is itself underperforming; first restore its SKU economics through eligible pricing and discount discipline before encouraging migration into it. Target deteriorating Synthetic Blend business, not an enterprise-wide repricing program. Preserve the operating practices in within-threshold periods 2026-006 through 2026-008; no well-performing product segment is identified for corrective intervention.
options_ranked.rationale: Price-volume-mix decomposition directs the intervention toward realized revenue rather than treating premium labels as evidence of profitability. Synthetic Blend's current 20.64% margin exceeds Conventional Engine Oil's 19.16% and Value's 19.82%, but these averages do not establish SKU-level migration economics. The contractual exclusion makes targeted pricing actionable without assuming blanket repricing authority; cross-product mix benefits are excluded from the segment recovery estimate.
options_ranked.time_to_value: First eligible price and incentive changes within 30 days; initial recovery within 0–90 days, with anchor-account changes deferred until contractual eligibility.

arguments_for: Price-volume-mix analysis supports targeting realized price and discount leakage because client-confirmed net revenue changes directly affect Gross Margin %.
arguments_against: The Stage 1 assumptions that 40–50% of business is eligible and customers accept 8–12% increases are not supported by supplied account evidence.
key_questions: Which eligible contracts can receive changes immediately without altering locked anchor-account economics?

arguments_for: The confirmed revenue-to-margin relationship permits recovery without waiting for procurement savings or manufacturing changes.
arguments_against: A price increase can be offset by customer concessions, smaller orders or higher cost to serve, so invoiced increases are not equivalent to retained margin.
key_questions: Will the commercial approval gate protect realized contribution after freight, rebates and order-size changes?

arguments_for: Selective incentive changes are reversible and preserve participation while testing whether affected Synthetic Blend demand remains economically attractive.
arguments_against: Synthetic Blend also deteriorated materially, so moving volume into it solely because of a premium designation would optimize an unverified portfolio assumption.
key_questions: Which destination SKUs exceed the contribution of displaced products after all incentives and incremental service costs?

implementation_triggers: Release a price change only when the contract owner confirms that the account is outside the anchor price lock or has reached its permitted repricing date.
Release migration incentives only after the destination SKU's post-change contribution exceeds that of the displaced SKU.
Suspend expansion if retained contribution falls below the approved account-level floor.
prerequisites: Sales Operations must exclude locked anchor accounts from mid-quarter list-price changes and preserve their contracted rebate and service terms.
The commercial approval package must distinguish within-Synthetic Blend recovery from any separate enterprise mix benefit.
Finance must sign the contribution floors using the completed analysis and applicable contract economics; this is an execution control, not a new analytics program.

impact_estimate.basis: The retained Stage 1 scenario recovers 3.5–5.2 percentage points of Synthetic Blend Engine Oil's 7.14-point decline through eligible price realization and within-segment incentive changes, implying a segment margin of 24.14–25.84%, not an enterprise forecast.

key_assumptions.assumption: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil has a recoverable observed margin gap of 7.14 percentage points.
key_assumptions.provenance: The named change point reports a decline from 27.78% to 20.64%.

key_assumptions.assumption: Enough revenue is contractually eligible for pricing changes within 90 days to support material recovery.
key_assumptions.provenance: The approved contract release schedule and eligible revenue share will confirm or falsify this assumption.

key_assumptions.assumption: Customers will accept price changes without contribution-destroying volume losses or concessions.
key_assumptions.provenance: Realized prices, retained orders and concessions on the first repriced contracts will test this assumption.

key_assumptions.assumption: Incentive changes can produce incremental within-Synthetic Blend margin beyond eligible price recovery.
key_assumptions.provenance: Post-incentive SKU contribution and mix must improve without equivalent rebate leakage or cannibalization.

flagged_side_effects: Poorly targeted incentives could shift demand into Synthetic Blend SKUs whose premium positioning does not translate into superior contribution.

options_ranked.title: Synthetic Blend Supplier Consolidation and Input-Cost Protection
options_ranked.description: Consolidate qualified Synthetic Blend base-oil purchases into negotiated supplier agreements with lower delivered unit costs, supported by bounded forward coverage for committed demand. Use supplier-linked pricing protection where feasible; financial hedges require explicit basis-risk and treasury approval. The operational solution is procurement execution, not a procurement audit. Target Synthetic Blend first, with Conventional Engine Oil and Compressor Oil eligible for separate sourcing work packages only where the same approved input specification applies. Leave within-threshold periods and any unaffected contracts outside corrective changes; the input supplies no healthy product benchmark to replicate.
options_ranked.rationale: Cost-to-serve and procurement methods pull the client-confirmed base-oil-cost-to-COGS-to-margin chain without changing locked selling prices. Parallel product declines are consistent with a shared cost pressure but do not identify its cause. Procurement savings must therefore come from executable delivered-cost reductions; locking today's input price protects against future deterioration but does not reverse historical inflation.
options_ranked.time_to_value: Supplier commitments and initial protection within 30–90 days; full realized savings depend on inventory turnover and supplier qualification.

arguments_for: Lower delivered COGS can protect contribution on anchor accounts that cannot receive mid-quarter list-price increases.
arguments_against: Supplier savings do not repair discount leakage or unattractive customer terms if realized pricing is the dominant source of deterioration.
key_questions: Will negotiated savings remain with the business rather than flow automatically into customer rebates or indexed selling prices?

arguments_for: Base oil is a client-confirmed COGS component, and COGS directly affects Gross Margin % at fixed revenue.
arguments_against: Neither a base-oil price increase nor available supplier savings is quantified in the input, and crude-linked hedges may poorly match base-oil purchase prices.
key_questions: Do executable supplier terms reduce delivered costs sufficiently after qualification expenses, hedge premiums and inventory carrying costs?

arguments_for: Bounded purchase coverage preserves the ability to change the portfolio while protecting committed customer demand.
arguments_against: Long minimum-purchase commitments could preserve exposure to weak products and increase exit costs.
key_questions: Can supplier volume commitments be capped at contracted demand and transferred across qualified formulations?

implementation_triggers: Award consolidated purchases only when landed costs beat the approved baseline after all fees and inventory costs.
Execute forward coverage only against approved demand and within treasury exposure limits.
Release new sources only after technical qualification and continuity-of-supply approval.
prerequisites: Procurement must obtain executable supplier concessions rather than count avoided future inflation as recovered margin.
Treasury must approve instrument suitability, basis risk, collateral requirements and maximum tenor.
Operations must maintain an approved alternative source and formulation quality.

impact_estimate.basis: The retained Stage 1 scenario recovers 3.5–5.8 percentage points of Synthetic Blend Engine Oil's 7.14-point loss through lower delivered input costs, requiring approximately 4.41–7.31% lower total segment COGS at unchanged revenue; forward protection alone does not create this recovery.

key_assumptions.assumption: Reducing base-oil costs reduces COGS and improves Gross Margin % when revenue is unchanged.
key_assumptions.provenance: Client-confirmed relationships identify base oil as a COGS component and COGS as a direct determinant of Gross Margin %.

key_assumptions.assumption: Supplier consolidation can deliver total segment COGS savings equivalent to 4.41–7.31%.
key_assumptions.provenance: Signed delivered-cost terms and subsequent consumption costs must demonstrate the required total-COGS reduction.

key_assumptions.assumption: Qualified suppliers can absorb consolidated orders without quality or continuity losses.
key_assumptions.provenance: Supplier commitments, qualification releases and on-time conforming deliveries will test capacity and quality.

key_assumptions.assumption: Forward protection can match the timing and price exposure of committed base-oil consumption.
key_assumptions.provenance: Settlement costs compared with actual purchase prices and consumption volumes will reveal basis and volume mismatches.

flagged_side_effects: Forward commitments can create collateral needs, excess inventory or losses when demand or input prices fall.

options_ranked.title: Contribution-Gated Value-Tier SKU Rationalization
options_ranked.description: Stop discretionary promotion of demonstrably unattractive Value-tier engine-oil SKUs, discontinue eligible low-contribution variants at contractual exit windows, and redirect released capacity only to verified higher-contribution formulations. Do not broadly de-emphasize Synthetic Blend: its 20.64% current margin exceeds Conventional Engine Oil's 19.16%. Full Synthetic and High Mileage destination margins are absent from the evidence, while Compressor Oil has a higher current margin of 28% but also declined by 5.86 points and is not an assumed demand substitute. If a proposed destination is underperforming, restore its realized price or delivered-cost economics before expanding it. Preserve profitable premium SKUs and within-threshold periods; no supplied product benchmark supports quantified practice replication.
options_ranked.rationale: Portfolio participation and exit economics address whether demand is worth serving rather than assuming every margin decline warrants restoration. However, the observed changes do not establish structural decline, and Synthetic Blend's premium margin advantage is only an unconfirmed industry prior. The proposal therefore replaces category-wide withdrawal with contribution-gated SKU decisions and a mandatory destination-economics gate; the retained impact range remains an unvalidated scenario, not an executable recovery commitment.
options_ranked.time_to_value: Initial promotion withdrawals within 30–90 days where permitted; SKU exits and capacity reallocation within 3–12 months.

arguments_for: Customer profitability analysis supports withdrawing discretionary support from SKUs that destroy contribution after rebates and service costs.
arguments_against: Removing entry-tier products can reduce customer basket value, impair channel relationships and cannibalize retained premium sales.
key_questions: Which exits preserve total customer contribution after substitution and lost cross-sales?

arguments_for: SKU rationalization can reduce avoidable changeovers, purchasing fragmentation and service complexity.
arguments_against: Allocated overhead may remain after exits, worsening absorption on retained products even if reported portfolio mix improves.
key_questions: Which costs will actually be removed, by which closure or resource-release action, before each SKU exits?

arguments_for: Participation analysis creates an independent route for persistently unattractive SKUs without assuming that price or procurement can repair every offering.
arguments_against: The input provides neither structural demand-decline evidence nor verified alternative-product economics, so a broad category retreat is not justified.
key_questions: Does each proposed replacement generate more retained contribution and cash after transition costs than continuing the existing SKU?

implementation_triggers: Withdraw discretionary promotions only when the SKU fails an approved contribution floor and contractual terms permit the change.
Approve migration only when destination contribution exceeds displaced contribution after incentives, incremental costs and cannibalization.
Authorize discontinuation only after customer obligations, inventory disposition and avoidable-cost removal are approved.
prerequisites: Finance must validate existing SKU-level contribution calculations before any volume is moved away from Synthetic Blend.
Sales must secure feasible substitutions rather than assume engine-oil demand can migrate to industrial products.
Operations must pair each exit with specific avoidable-cost actions and an inventory disposition plan.
Anchor-account list prices remain unchanged mid-quarter, and contracted supply obligations must be honored.

impact_estimate.basis: The retained Stage 1 enterprise composition scenario proposes 3.5–5.8 percentage points through selective SKU exits and verified higher-margin replacements, but against the reported 4.49-point enterprise decline its upper bound exceeds recovery by 1.31 points and is unsupported without revenue weights and destination margins.

key_assumptions.assumption: Synthetic Blend currently earns a higher average gross margin than Conventional Engine Oil.
key_assumptions.provenance: Named change points show Synthetic Blend at 20.64% and Conventional Engine Oil at 19.16%.

key_assumptions.assumption: Some targeted SKUs have persistently unattractive avoidable contribution rather than merely unfavorable overhead allocations.
key_assumptions.provenance: Approved exit cases must show negative or sub-threshold retained contribution after separating avoidable and stranded costs.

key_assumptions.assumption: Higher-contribution substitute products exist and can absorb profitable customer demand.
key_assumptions.provenance: Accepted customer substitutions and destination SKU contribution after transition costs will test this assumption.

key_assumptions.assumption: Reducing selected Synthetic Blend volumes will not destroy a larger premium-mix benefit.
key_assumptions.provenance: The post-substitution portfolio contribution bridge must exceed the retained-Synthetic-Blend case; the supplied premium-mix relationship is an unconfirmed prior.

key_assumptions.assumption: Released capacity and avoidable costs can be removed or redeployed within the implementation horizon.
key_assumptions.provenance: Executed capacity transfers, staffing changes and canceled expenditure must match each approved exit case.

flagged_side_effects: Reducing Synthetic Blend exposure could remove profitable premium sales and lower Gross Margin % rather than restore it; contribution validation is mandatory before reallocation.
Portfolio Gross Margin % can rise while absolute gross profit, revenue and cash generation fall.
SKU exits can strand overhead and inventory or breach service commitments if implemented before contractual exit windows.

Procurement remains an independent alternative whose recovery depends on unverified cost concessions, while portfolio reallocation retains an enterprise upper estimate above the observed 4.49-point loss. Authorize only the bounded eligible-account rollout, not a commitment to the full 3.5–5.2-point scenario or a consensus program combining all three options.

problem_reframe.situation: Gross Margin % declined year to date. The problem statement reports a 7.14 percentage-point drop to 20.64%, but those values match Synthetic Blend Engine Oil specifically; the deep-analysis headline reports an overall decline of 4.49 points, from 34.43% to 29.94%. Segment recovery and enterprise recovery must therefore be distinguished.
problem_reframe.complication: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil, Conventional Engine Oil and Compressor Oil deteriorated by 7.14, 6.61 and 5.86 points, respectively. The supplied temporal evidence is mixed: periods 2026-006, 2026-007 and 2026-008 show positive changes and are classified as within threshold. No outperforming product benchmark, where_is_not list, revenue weights or comparison-versus-plan results are supplied. Mid-quarter list-price increases on anchor accounts are prohibited, and neither input-cost inflation nor structural category decline is established by the segment margin changes alone.
problem_reframe.question: Which bounded intervention should receive authorization to restore Gross Margin % without breaching anchor-account price locks, confusing segment and enterprise impacts, or sacrificing profitable premium business?

key_assumptions.assumption: The 7.14-point deterioration describes Synthetic Blend Engine Oil rather than the entire business.

commercial.framework: Price-Volume-Mix Decomposition with COGS Waterfall Analysis
commercial.hypothesis: Gross margin compression of 7.14 percentage points in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil is driven primarily by elevated base oil costs (confirmed COGS component) flowing through to COGS without corresponding price recovery, exacerbated by potential mix shift toward lower-priced SKUs within the Synthetic Blend category. The Value segment's -6.42 pp decline corroborates a volume-driven, lower-tier mix effect masking what should be structurally higher-margin premium formulations.
key_evidence: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin fell 7.14 pp (27.78% → 20.64%) year-to-date, representing the largest single product-level deterioration and accounting for the portfolio's total margin loss

Conventional Engine Oil declined 6.61 pp (25.77% → 19.16%), indicating the pressure is not isolated to premium tiers; base oil cost inflation is hitting both segments uniformly, suggesting commodity input cost as the common driver

Value category segment margin declined 6.42 pp (26.24% → 19.82%), indicating revenue is shifting toward lower-priced tier or volume is concentrating in discount-sensitive channels, compounding the COGS pressure rather than offsetting it through mix-up

operational.framework: Cost-to-Serve Analysis with Input-Cost Hedging Diagnostics
operational.hypothesis: Gross margin compression of 7.14 percentage points in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil is primarily driven by unhedged base oil cost inflation, not volume or mix effects. The 7-point delta mirrors typical synthetic blend formulation cost sensitivity (40–50% base oil input cost as % of COGS). Conventional Engine Oil follows with a -6.61 delta, confirming oil-input-cost as the common mechanism. The 'Value' product category delta of -6.42 further corroborates this: lower-tier products have narrower margin buffers and absorb input-cost shocks more visibly.
key_evidence: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin fell 7.14 points (27.78% → 20.64%) while Conventional Engine Oil fell 6.61 points (25.77% → 19.16%), indicating a shared cost driver rather than product-specific demand or pricing pressure.

Both oil grades and the 'Value' category segment show synchronized margin erosion (deltas: -7.14, -6.61, -6.42), consistent with a commodity input cost shock rather than localized volume or mix distortion.

Compressor Oil (delta: -5.86) also affected, extending the signal across all oil-type product_names—pattern incompatible with SKU-level demand loss or discounting, pointing to base oil procurement cost as the common denominator.

structural.framework: Portfolio Participation Analysis × Structural Decline vs. Cyclical Dip

This is NOT a pricing/volume variance recoverable via KPI optimization—it reflects category-level input cost inflation or forced reallocation away from higher-margin synthetic formulations.

Segment recovery of 3.5–5.2 points remains within Synthetic Blend's 7.14-point decline and implies 24.14–25.84% margin, below its previous 27.78%; however, the Stage 1 price and eligibility assumptions alone support only approximately 2.46–4.49 points, so the full range remains conditional on additional realized incentive benefits.

opt_3.causal_grounding: net_revenue -> gross_margin_pct and cogs -> gross_margin_pct: portfolio exits and substitutions change revenue composition and retained costs; the sign and size of the effect are conditional on destination economics and avoidable costs.

proposed_option.title: Targeted SKU-Level Price Indexation on Synthetic Blend Premium Tiers + Mix Incentive Rebalancing
proposed_option.description: Within the contractual price-lock constraint on anchor accounts, implement a tiered price recovery on Synthetic Blend formulations (e.g., High Mileage, Extended Drain variants) targeting non-anchor or renewal-cycle accounts. Simultaneously, restructure distributor/retail incentive programs to shift volume mix away from Value-tier SKUs toward higher-margin Synthetic Blend grades, recovering the 7.14 pp margin loss through dual mechanism: selective price lift on premium SKUs + volume reallocation.
proposed_option.mechanism: Base oil cost inflation (confirmed COGS driver) has eroded margin uniformly across products. Price-lock constraints prevent blanket repricing, but selective indexation on Synthetic Blend premium SKUs (which carry structurally higher margins) can recover margin dollars without breaching anchor account terms. Simultaneously, incentive rebalancing redirects volume from Value-tier (lower-margin) SKUs to premium Synthetic Blend, improving blended mix and offsetting commodity cost pressure through volume composition rather than pure price.

impact_estimate.basis: Synthetic Blend is the largest driver (7.14 pp loss). Selective price indexation targeting 8–12% uplift on premium SKUs (assuming 40–50% of Synthetic Blend volume qualifies outside anchor lock) recovers ~2.5–3.5 pp. Mix rebalancing toward Synthetic Blend from Value tier (6.42 pp decline) can capture 1.0–1.7 pp through volume shift, totaling 3.5–5.2 pp gross margin % recovery.

proposed_option.title: Base Oil Cost Hedging & Procurement Consolidation for Synthetic Blends
proposed_option.description: Conduct an urgent procurement audit of base oil sourcing for Synthetic Blend formulations, quantify the YTD cost-per-unit inflation vs. prior-year benchmarks, and execute a 90-day forward hedge (futures, supplier contracts, or inventory-timing strategies) to lock in current or forward-curve pricing. Simultaneously, consolidate supplier orders to improve negotiating leverage and reduce fragmented sourcing inefficiency.
proposed_option.mechanism: Base oil represents 40–50% of COGS in synthetic blend lubricants. A 15–20% spike in crude-derived base oil costs (plausible in current commodity environment) directly translates to a 6–10 percentage point margin hit if selling prices are locked by contract. Hedging locks input cost, protecting margin until contract renewal or commercial renegotiation windows open post-Q2.

impact_estimate.basis: Synthetic Blend delta is -7.14 pp; a 50–80% recovery via input-cost stabilization (hedging + procurement leverage) yields 3.5–5.7 pp uplift. Conservative estimate assumes partial hedge execution and 1–2 month lag to full effect. Conventional Oil recovery potential: 3.3–4.9 pp (proportional to its -6.61 delta).

proposed_option.title: Structural Category Reallocation: De-emphasize Value-Tier Engine Oils, Redirect Volume to Margin-Accretive Formulations or Exit Low-Margin SKUs
proposed_option.description: Rather than attempt to recover margin through pricing (contractually blocked) or volume levers (upstream cost inflation will persist), reallocate portfolio emphasis away from Conventional and Synthetic Blend grades in the Value category toward higher-margin synthetic or specialty formulations, or selectively exit low-margin SKUs where base oil cost inflation has eroded structural profitability. This reframes the problem from 'how do we fix margin on these products' to 'do these products belong in our portfolio at current cost structures.'
proposed_option.mechanism: By reducing sales mix exposure to Synthetic Blend and Conventional grades (which now carry structurally depressed margins due to base oil cost or distribution cost inflation), the blended portfolio gross margin % recovers through composition, not through fixing individual product margins. This assumes higher-margin alternatives (e.g., Full Synthetic, High Mileage, or specialty formulations) exist in the portfolio and can absorb volume reallocation without cannibalizing revenue.

impact_estimate.basis: Synthetic Blend and Conventional together account for the largest deltas (-7.14pp and -6.61pp). If reallocation reduces their contribution to blended margin by 50% and redirects that volume to formulations with 5–7pp higher margins, portfolio gross margin recovers 3.5–5.8pp. Conservative estimate reflects volume absorption constraints and potential revenue headwinds from de-emphasis.
